clue.text: Old men with heads together pulled apart, glaring

indicators.note: each pa's head is its first letter; for the two heads to meet, the first pa is turned round so its P sits next to the other's

parts.note: one's old man is one's father, pa
the plural asks for a second old man, another pa
rent means torn, pulled apart

explanation.surface: Two elderly men butting heads have to be separated, plainly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with heads together' turns the first PA round to AP, so the two P's, their heads, touch in APPA.
explanation.definitionFit: Glaring means obvious, as in a glaring error, so it matches something plainly evident.

clue.text: Quickly drop crumbs in empty pot

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so these letters are lodged between the two that survive beside them
a container called empty has had everything between its walls taken out, so only the letters at the two ends are left

parts.note: the vessel emptied of its insides keeps only its first and last letters
'crumbs!' and 'lumme!' are the same mild British cry of surprise, lumme being a worn-down 'lord love me'

explanation.surface: Dropping crumbs into a pot with nothing in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crumbs' is not the food but the exclamation, and it is swapped for another exclamation almost nobody says any more. Both belong to a politely startled kind of British English.
explanation.definitionFit: To plummet is to fall fast and straight down, so 'quickly drop' is the same verb with the speed built into it.

clue.text: Protection English and American soldier wear equally

indicators.note: what you wear goes round the outside of the wearer, so the letters named after this word wrap themselves about the ones named before it

parts.note: as tall as, as good as: 'as' is the little word that says two things measure the same, and it opens up round what it covers
E is the standard abbreviation for English
a GI is an American private soldier, from 'government issue'

explanation.surface: English and American troops turning out in identical kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wear' sits in the sentence as the soldiers' uniform and works as the instruction to wrap. The word itself is Greek: the aegis was the shield Zeus carried, which is why it now means somebody's protection.
explanation.definitionFit: Under someone's aegis you are under their protection or sponsorship, the sense that outlived the shield the word started as.

clue.text: Euro Senor tossed bum

indicators.note: something tossed is thrown up and lands however it lands, which is what happens to the letters it is holding

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: A euro tossed to a Spanish gentleman turns out to be a bad one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum' is the adjective, not the noun: a bum steer, bum information. Senor keeps a Spanish look right up to the point where it hands over ordinary letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A bum steer is wrong information, so 'bum' is the informal adjective for mistaken that this nine-letter word states formally.

clue.text: Heel pain occupies mind

indicators.note: to occupy a space is to sit inside it, so these letters take up room in the middle of the word beside them

parts.note: to mind a shop or a child is to tend it
whatever ails you is giving you pain, and the verb supplies three letters

explanation.surface: An aching heel filling somebody's thoughts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heel' is the last inch of a loaf, not the back of a foot, which is how a two-word answer comes to define it. 'Mind' and 'tend' are the same verb of looking after.
explanation.definitionFit: The heel of a loaf is its very last piece, and the tail end of anything is that same final scrap.

clue.text: Cryptic equivalent of temperature into Celsius?

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for Celsius on any thermometer
'four into twelve' is the schoolroom way of saying twelve divided by four, and a division is written as one number over another
T is the standard abbreviation for temperature

explanation.surface: A quiz question about converting a temperature into Celsius.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the setter owning up: 'into' is not an insertion here but arithmetic, and division is the one operation you write as a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Cryptic and covert both mean deliberately hidden: a covert operation is kept out of sight, and a cryptic remark keeps its meaning out of sight.

clue.text: Copper that takes the biscuit showing restraint?

definitions.note: The answer is a plural noun and the definition is a participle phrase, which is what the question mark concedes: the joke is that these things show restraint by applying it, not by exercising self-control.

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper, from the Latin cuprum
something that takes the biscuit beats everything, and FFS is the texted expletive of exasperation fired back at it

explanation.surface: A policeman who is the absolute limit, yet holding back.
explanation.walkthrough: Copper is the metal, not the policeman the surface is selling, and the second half is not a definition at all but a whole exclamation shortened the way a phone would shorten it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuffs are handcuffs, the restraints an officer carries, and the question mark flags the pun: they show restraint by holding somebody still.

clue.text: Rivals tee off, good all round

indicators.note: someone whose aim is off has gone astray, and letters sent astray come back in a different order

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Golfers driving off the first tee in fine all-round form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tee off' reads as one golfing phrase and has to be split: the tee joins the fodder and 'off' does the shuffling. 'Good all round' sounds like praise for a sportsman and is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone versatile can turn a hand to anything, which is exactly the claim made by calling a player good all round.

clue.text: University dons party after dealing with surplus

indicators.note: the party piece with its insert comes after the short word for concerning

parts.note: re means concerning or dealing with

indicators.note: to don is to put on, so the party piece is worn round the university letter

parts.note: a side is a party in a dispute or contest

explanation.surface: University lecturers throw a party after handling the extra money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dons' looks like academics but is the verb: SIDE wraps round U to give SIDUE.
explanation.definitionFit: Residue is what is left over, the remainder or excess.

clue.text: Chuck's ready to corrupt official, perhaps

definitions.meaning: the informal verb for throwing something without taking much care over it
the ready is old slang for cash in hand, and cash pressed on an official to bend a decision has its own name in football reporting

explanation.surface: Chuck has the cash to bribe an official.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chuck' sits at the front of the sentence looking like a man's name and is a verb. The whole of the rest of the clue is the second definition, resting on 'the ready' meaning money.
explanation.definitionFit: To chuck something is to bung it, informally; and a bung is the wad of ready money slipped to an official to buy a decision.

clue.text: Artist chosen to replace Parisian is soaking wood

parts.note: an RA is a Royal Academician, the crossword's standard artist
a player chosen for the team is in
a substitute comes on for the player going off, which is 'for' meaning in place of
'est' is the French for 'is', so a Parisian says it

explanation.surface: A painter picked to stand in for a French one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To replace' looks like an instruction to swap something over and is only the word 'for'. Nothing in this clue asks you to do anything: four short words are each traded for a shorter one and laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: A rainforest is woodland soaked by constant rain, so 'soaking wood' describes it literally rather than by any figure of speech.

clue.text: Take wrong street with east of motorway split

indicators.note: east is to the right on any map, and in an across entry the letters to the right are the ones written later

parts.note: the M1 runs north out of London, and in a grid its number does duty as the letter I
to sunder something is to split it in two
ST is the standard abbreviation for street
bread with butter, bread and butter: the two words join things in the same way

explanation.surface: Taking the wrong street east of where the motorway divides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take wrong' is a verb phrase, not a driving error, and that is the whole misdirection, since every other word is doing map work. Road numbers become letters freely in grids, which have no squares for digits.
explanation.definitionFit: To take something wrong is to misunderstand it, 'take' being the sense in which you take a remark badly.

clue.text: Plaster commanding officers put on wounds in retreat

indicators.note: put on means the officer is placed after the other piece
in retreat means going backwards, so the letters are read from right to left

parts.note: cuts are wounds
CO is the abbreviation for commanding officer

explanation.surface: Officers dress soldiers' wounds during a withdrawal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in retreat' reaches back only to the wounds, not the officers, who keep their usual order.
explanation.definitionFit: Stucco is a fine plaster used to coat walls and make mouldings.

clue.text: Uncle Tom, terrible yankee insult

indicators.note: a terrible mess is a thing in complete disorder, and letters in disorder have to be set down in a new arrangement

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
Y is yankee in the phonetic alphabet used over the radio

explanation.surface: Calling somebody an Uncle Tom, which is a dreadful American insult.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface is an insult, which hides the fact that only the letters of two of them matter. Contumely is Hamlet's word, from 'the proud man's contumely', and it means abuse heaped on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Contumely is insulting language or scornful abuse, so 'insult' names it as a noun, though it survives now mostly in that soliloquy.

clue.text: Stripped, dive deeper at sea using half the energy

indicators.note: a swimmer at sea is adrift with nothing to hold position by, so the letters lose the order they arrived in
energy is E, four of them are handed over, and only half that many are used

parts.note: the ten letters of the two words with two of their four Es dropped, leaving eight

explanation.surface: Free divers going down further on less air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stripped' looks exactly like an anagram signal and is the definition instead, so the word you would reach for first is the one word not giving an instruction. The Es are counted, not chosen.
explanation.definitionFit: To be deprived of something is to have been stripped of it, and both are past participles for having had a thing taken away.

clue.text: Food for retail earlier cleared out

parts.note: the pros and cons are the fors and againsts
to vend something is to retail it, as a vending machine does

indicators.note: a room cleared out has had everything between its walls carried away, so only the two ends are left standing

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word, everything between them cleared away

explanation.surface: A shop that sold food having been emptied earlier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Food for retail' reads as one phrase off a wholesaler's invoice, and the definition stops dead after the first word. Provender is the old word for fodder: feed for animals, and by extension supplies for people.
explanation.definitionFit: Provender is fodder, the feed put by for livestock and by extension the provisions people store, so 'food' names the general kind.

clue.text: Despite arrangement, doesn't date pay for drink?

parts.note: to stand somebody a drink is to pay for it
to sup is to drink, the old northern verb still heard in 'supping ale'

explanation.surface: Somebody who made an arrangement and then neither turns up nor pays for the drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs on for five words and the wordplay is only the last three, which is why the join is so hard to find. Both halves of the wordplay are pub verbs, so the sentence never changes subject.
explanation.definitionFit: To arrange a date and then not appear is to stand somebody up, and the definition is that failure to show, put in the third person.

clue.text: Pedant not starting difficult puzzle

indicators.note: a word not starting has not got its opening letter, so that first one never appears

parts.note: a stickler is somebody who insists on a rule down to the last detail

explanation.surface: A pedant who will not begin a hard crossword.
explanation.walkthrough: A tickler is a problem that teases you, the clue that sits unsolved half the morning, and the surface pretends the pedant is simply too grand to start one.
explanation.definitionFit: A tickler is a poser, a problem that keeps niggling at you, so the noun phrase names the thing rather than describing it.

clue.text: That could be a hot spring rising

parts.note: per means a, each, as in five pounds a head

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means the letters read from the bottom upwards, reversed

parts.note: a spa is a mineral spring
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A spa guide speculates that a geyser might be a hot spring coming up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' looks like a throwaway article but is PER; 'rising' turns SPA + H into HAPS under it.
explanation.definitionFit: Perhaps expresses possibility, the same sense as saying something might be so.

clue.text: Too old really to snort line

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old

indicators.note: a line snorted is drawn up inside the person taking it, so this letter goes inside the word beside it

parts.note: really good, very good: the two intensifiers do the same job
L is the standard abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: An elderly person really snorting a line of cocaine.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface is about drugs and every word of the wordplay is about grammar. 'Too' is the adverb of excess, as in too keen, not the one meaning 'as well'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Too' in the sense of excessively, as in too keen, is exactly what this adverb means, and it is not the first sense that comes to mind.

clue.text: Doctor dwelt on disappointing outcome

indicators.note: to doctor a document is to tamper with it, so what stands beside it comes out altered

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: A doctor who kept going on about a poor result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is the very first word and reads as a person, which is where setters most like to hide the instruction. 'Dwelt on' is a phrase in its own right and is only letters here.
explanation.definitionFit: A letdown is an outcome that falls short of what was promised, the noun for the flat feeling left behind.

clue.text: Opposing force tally with crew on Queen Elizabeth

indicators.note: one thing set on another in an across entry is written after it, so the pieces named before this word follow the one named after it

parts.note: to tally votes is to count them
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the royal monogram on British postboxes and stamps
W is the standard abbreviation for with
an eight is the standard racing boat rowed at Henley, so its crew and its name are the same number

explanation.surface: The ship's company mustering aboard the liner Queen Elizabeth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crew' means the number eight because a rowing eight is a boatload, a piece of British sporting shorthand worth keeping. The liner in the surface has nothing to do with the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A counterweight is the mass hung on the far side to pull against a load, so 'opposing force' names the job it does.

clue.text: Criminal group lasered air traffic from beneath shelters

indicators.note: a down entry picked up from its foot comes from beneath, so the letters are collected in that upward direction
to shelter something is to keep it hidden inside, and these words are keeping letters between them

parts.note: five consecutive letters run from the end of the first word across the second, and they are collected from the far end backwards

explanation.surface: Gangsters aiming lasers at aircraft from under cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal group lasered' reads as a headline about a gang being targeted, and it is really the definition followed by the start of the hiding place. Triads are the Chinese crime syndicates of Hong Kong and beyond.
explanation.definitionFit: A triad is one of those Chinese criminal societies, so 'criminal group' names the class it belongs to rather than defining the word.

clue.text: Dieter's good sandwiches are primarily meat spread

indicators.note: the German word holds the next letters between its own, like bread round a filling

parts.note: Dieter is a typical German name, and gut is German for good
an are is a metric unit of area, abbreviated A

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of meat is used

parts.note: the word meat supplies its opening letter

explanation.surface: A slimmer's healthy sandwiches turn out to be mostly meat spread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dieter' is not a slimmer but a German name, so his 'good' is GUT. 'sandwiches' puts A (the are, a unit of area) and M (first of meat, by 'primarily') inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A gamut is the full range or spread of something, as in running the gamut of emotions.

clue.text: Atlantic voyage's record Iand-lubber sabotaged with hidden typo?

indicators.note: sabotaged means wrecked, so the letters are thrown into a new order
the clue admits that its word carries a concealed misprint, I for L, and the letters are used as printed

parts.note: landlubber, someone unused to the sea, printed with a capital I in place of its first L

explanation.surface: A sea record spoiled by a lubber who sabotaged it, with a sly misprint slipped in.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital I in 'Iand-lubber' looks like an L, which is what 'with hidden typo' owns up to; 'sabotaged' then rearranges IANDLUBBER. The Blue Riband was the honour for the fastest Atlantic crossing by a liner.
explanation.definitionFit: The Blue Riband was the unofficial accolade held by the passenger liner with the fastest Atlantic crossing, a speed record.

clue.text: Usually high area's right next to low

indicators.note: one thing next to another is written alongside it, so the two pieces simply run together

parts.note: cattle low, and the noise they make is spelt this way
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A weather map with an area of high pressure right beside a low.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a forecast, high pressure beside low, and 'low' is the cow instead. 'Usually' is the setter conceding that not every stretch of this ground is upland.
explanation.definitionFit: A moor is rough open upland, the high ground of the Pennines and Dartmoor, and 'usually' allows for the boggy low-lying sort.

clue.text: Report of attack on unknown shot inside

parts.note: x is the unknown quantity in algebra

indicators.note: in an across entry one thing on another is written after it, so the sounded word follows the single letter

parts.note: an attack is a raid, and 'report of' asks for the sound of the word rather than its spelling

explanation.surface: News of an attack on someone unidentified who was shot indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' does two jobs: a news report of an attack, and the signal that a sound is wanted. 'Shot' is a photograph, which is the other half of the trap.
explanation.definitionFit: Something x-rayed has been photographed from the inside out, so 'shot inside' is that picture taken as a verb.

clue.text: Wee behind bushes avoiding bachelor's gaze

indicators.note: behind means coming after, so the word for small follows the cut-down bushes
avoiding means keeping away from, so that letter is left out

parts.note: scrub is land covered with low bushes, or the bushes themselves
B is the abbreviation for bachelor, as in degrees like BA
wee is Scottish for small, tiny

explanation.surface: A man relieving himself in the bushes tries to escape a bachelor's stare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wee' is not what the surface suggests but small, TINY; 'avoiding' drops B from SCRUB, and 'behind' sets TINY after SCRU.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrutiny is close, searching examination, a hard look at something.
